nameStory: The spinybacked orbweaver gets its name from the sharp, thorn-like spines that stick out from its abdomen like a medieval shield. Its scientific name tells the same story - 'Gasteracantha' comes from ancient Greek words meaning 'belly' and 'thorn,' while 'cancriformis' means 'crab-shaped' in Latin, describing its wide, spiny appearance.
description: This is one of nature's most unusual-looking spiders, instantly recognizable by the six sharp spines jutting out from its wide, flat abdomen. The spinybacked orbweaver is a small spider, with females reaching about the size of a dime including the spines. Despite its fearsome appearance, it's completely harmless to humans and creates beautiful, classic orb webs like other orbweavers. The body is often brightly colored in combinations of white, yellow, orange, or red with black markings.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is dramatically wide and flat with six hard, pointed spines sticking out - three on each side - making it look like a tiny crab or shield

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic sticky orb webs that feel slightly thicker and more substantial than those of common garden spiders, often positioned in shrubs or between plants

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females are small - about 5-9mm wide not counting spines, roughly the size of a pencil eraser, while males are even tinier

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Brightly colored abdomen often featuring white, yellow, or orange backgrounds with distinctive black spots or patterns that can vary considerably

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits in the center of its web during the day, and when disturbed, the hard spines make a slight clicking sound if touched gently with a stick

habitat: In New England, this southern species is extremely rare and found only in the warmest microclimates, typically in protected gardens, greenhouses, or very sheltered urban areas in the southernmost regions. When present, they prefer shrubs and low vegetation where they can string their webs between branches about 2-6 feet off the ground.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin appearing in late spring in the warmest locations, but are rarely observed in New England's cooler climate.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be spotted, though sightings remain extremely uncommon in our region.
seasonality.fall: Any remaining adults may persist into early fall before cold weather eliminates them, as they cannot survive New England winters.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent - this species cannot survive freezing temperatures and has no overwintering stage in New England.

funFact: The spines on this spider's back are actually part of its exoskeleton and are rock-hard - they're so tough that they often remain intact long after the spider dies, creating tiny natural sculptures that can last for months.
confusionNotes: Nothing else in New England looks remotely like this spider - those six spines make it unmistakable. If you see spines on a spider's back in our region, you've found something extremely rare!
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a southern species that's at the very northern edge of its range in New England. Most field guides focus on southern populations, so don't be surprised if you never encounter one - they're essentially tropical spiders pushing into temperate regions.
compareHints: This is the only spiny orbweaver species in our region, making comparison straightforward. Unlike other orbweavers in New England which have soft, rounded abdomens, the spinybacked orbweaver's hard, spiny shell makes it look more like a tiny armored vehicle than a typical spider. Other orbweavers might be larger or have different web patterns, but none have anything resembling these dramatic spines.
